memory_candidates.content: When applying a semantic-anchor-finding authorization to a mechanical duplicate-block inventory, apply it in BOTH directions. A literal-text shingling test both under-counts genuine prose anchors (wording drift) AND over-counts collapse candidates: a matched window that is a mandatory format-schema heading (every instance of a file-type MUST carry it to be compliant), a complete worked YAML/JSON/bash example a reader needs in place, a reference table that IS the lookup content, or a deliberately-documented mirror/parity copy (kept content-identical for a stated deploy-mechanism or standalone-availability reason) is NOT genuinely collapsible even though it matches the mechanical test. Across one markdown-consolidation phase, 13 of 15 mechanically-flagged rows fell into one of these four classes; only 2 were genuine restateable prose. Check each matched window's actual surrounding context (is it inside a code fence? is it a schema the format itself requires? does the file's own prose explain why it must stay duplicated?) before collapsing, not just whether the text matches.

A script that reconciles a manifest's declared file list against the filesystem (e.g. sync-manifest-scripts.sh) may enumerate 'files on disk' via `git ls-files` rather than a plain filesystem walk. A newly created file that is still untracked (not yet `git add`-ed) will NOT be seen as 'on disk' by such a script and will be silently skipped from its repair pass, even though the file genuinely exists. Stage new files with `git add` BEFORE running a git-ls-files-backed reconciliation/sync script, or its write-mode pass will miss them and a subsequent gate (e.g. a deployed-vs-source content-hash check) will fail on the untracked file once it is eventually staged elsewhere.
